newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African bond market reform seen gradual.
newsitem.headline: S.African bond market reform seen gradual.

text.p: Introduction of formal market-making in government bonds in South Africa is likely to be gradual as it would require major adjustments, a survey has found.

The survey, released to the parliamentary finance committee on Wednesday, was conducted in September last year by the finance department to sound out views on the introduction of regular bond auctions and shifting market making from the Reserve Bank to financial institutions.
The survey found that some broking firms were in favour of continuing with the present system because it was well understood, while the 14 day settlement period created necessary liquidity.
They also said that replacing the present system with a more capital intensive and expensive one could be difficult to justify in the light of the relatively small domestic market.

"These arguments are, however, countered by the view that the South African bond market is increasingly becoming part of the global market and it would be in its own interests to conform to internationally acceptable norms," the survey said.
These included greater liquidity, open price setting, a regulatory framework to protect traders and investors and a more efficient clearing, settlement and scrip system.

"Despite the strong support for the introduction of a formal system of market-making in government bonds, a gradual reform approach seems to be generally favoured in order not to risk undue disruption of the financial markets," the survey said.
Liquidity would be an important factor and this could be enhanced through the introduction of a repo market, benchmark bonds, futures contracts, stripping facilities and exchange traded options.

These would have to be accompanied by the gradual introduction of shorter settlement periods, an electronic scrip registry, central bank surveillance, risk management systems, minimum capital requirements, an efficient legal framework and a viable aucion processes.
"Changes from the existing procedures should however ensure that South African bonds could be handled by international investors' back office systems," the survey said.
Major issues that would have to be considered included whether both domestic and international institutions should be appointed as market makers, and how many market-makers should be appointed.

"The appropriate approach for the South African situation appears to be that no restriction should be placed on the number of market makers as long as they meet the specified prudential requirements and performance obligations," the survey said.

The new debt management office in the finance department would oversee market makers and bond issues, but should keep all participants fully informed about the public sector borrowing programme. No "special deal" arrangements and prices should be made.
The Reserve Bank would monitor the market and the survey found that it was believed that the relaxation of exchange controls would not have any major effect on the market.
The Bond Exchange would introduce a three day settlement period and further encourage the development of a bond futures market, the survey said.
